19933-cluthe-s-advice-to-the-ruptured:
Cluthe's Advice to the Ruptured is a medical advertising booklet about hernia. It compares rupture unfavorably with poor eyesight. Glasses that improve sight are easy enough to get, it says. Only a small share of rupture sufferers ever find real support. Most find nothing that even keeps the rupture from growing worse. The Cluthe truss is then offered as that rare support. Charles Cluthe's firm sold trusses from New Jersey for decades.

Before safe hernia surgery, trusses were the standard answer. Makers competed with booklets of advice and testimony. Cluthe's mixes anatomy, warning, and salesmanship in that order. Such ephemera document everyday medicine before hospitals dominated. The booklet survives as honest period quack-adjacent print. It shows sufferers addressed as customers first.
20330-the-black-wolf-s-breed:
The Black Wolf's Breed, from 1899, is a historical tale set under Louis XIV. Its people are king and courtier, soldier and diplomat, lass and lady. Brave fighting and loose swords fill the stage, the preface warns. Honor clings to an empty shadow in that glittering, faithless court.

The women seem more fair than honest, the writer adds with a shrug. He begs readers to recall when these things happened, and where. France under the Sun King gives the tale its pomp and peril. Readers get swashbuckling romance in a court of spies and swordsmen.
20866-infantry-drill-regulations-united-:
Distance, in drill terms, means the space from one man's back to the next man's breast. The 1911 Infantry Drill Regulations fix that gap at forty inches in line and column. Each term in the book gets that same crisp, fixed sense.

These rules governed how American infantry marched, formed, and fought in 1911. Officers drilled companies by its words on fields across the country. The corrected text shows an army on the edge of modern war. Students of military history can trace in it the last full bloom of close-order drill before machine guns rewrote the field.
21351-the-prayer-book-explained:
Percival Jackson of Jesus College, Cambridge, published the first part of The Prayer Book Explained in 1901. It covers the daily offices and the litany of the Church of England. He quotes Hooker at the start: the book requires but orderly reading. His preface defends the service book against easy distrust.

Jackson argues that the spirit of worship rests on faith in God, in the words used, and in the people worshipping together. He explains each office's structure and history for churchgoers who say the words weekly without knowing their roots. A second part was to follow on the rest of the Prayer Book.
21498-france-and-the-republic-a-record-o:
William Henry Hurlbert toured the French provinces in 1889 and wrote France and the Republic. The year was the centennial of the French Revolution, and the republic marked it in state. Hurlbert, who had written on Ireland under coercion, brought a sharp eye to France.

He weighs French republican rule against Swiss and American practice, and finds it wanting. Chapters treat Gambetta's rise, the powers of the executive, and the reach of the legislature. A map backs his record of things seen and learned on the road. The book is a frank, hostile tour of a young republic at one hundred years.
21738-hunted-and-harried:
Dragoons cross the river Cairn in Dumfriesshire on a bright morning in this Ballantyne tale of seventeenth-century Scotland. The troop rides for the moors near Skeoch Hill, mud-spattered from a long hunt. Their young officer rides ahead, and one trooper's face carries a sadness the others lack. They are hunting men, not game.

The story belongs to the years when Scotland's Covenanters were chased across their own hills for their faith. Ballantyne tells it from both sides of the hunt, soldier and fugitive. Faith, mercy, and cruelty meet on the moors in his telling. It is one of his most serious books, built on a dark and well-remembered page of Scottish history.
21843-the-botanical-magazine-vol-06-or-f:
Foreign flowers in their true colors fill this sixth volume of William Curtis's Botanical Magazine, the famous flower-garden journal. Each plant is drawn and colored from life, then described by name, class, and order in the system of Linnaeus. Curtis adds where each plant grows, when it flowers, and the best way to grow it. The work served ladies, gentlemen, and gardeners who wanted science with their pleasure.

Curtis had won fame with his Flora Londinensis before starting the magazine. Volume by volume, the series became the most loved botanical periodical in English. Gardeners still prize its plates for accuracy and beauty together. This volume keeps the standard: exact botany, plain culture advice, and flowers shown as they truly look.
21873-planet-of-the-damned:
Brion steps into a temple of hooded, empty-eyed men in Harry Harrison's Planet of the Damned. The story first ran in Analog magazine in 1961, then became a Bantam book in 1962. Something evil infects the planet, and the still figure at the room's center moves with crazy menace. Brion knows at once that he has found the enemy. The tale builds from that chill into full science fiction adventure.

Harrison, also author of the Deathworld books, writes fast and lean. His hero must grasp a whole world's madness before he can fight it. The book became a staple of paperback science fiction shelves. It shows Harrison's gift: a strange world, a hard problem, and a man thinking his way through both at speed.
21892-at-the-time-appointed:
A lonely mountain station under a fierce noonday sun opens A. Maynard Barbour's At the Time Appointed, first published in 1903. The line winds far above the level of the sea. A stranger dismounts there to meet a woman who comes swiftly toward him, hand extended. Barbour had won her readers with That Mainwaring Affair, praised in its day for thrills worthy of Anna Katharine Green.

Reviewers quoted on this edition stress the plot's adroit turns and the clean, excellent style. The story works as mystery without cheap sensation, they said. Darrell, the man of the frontispiece, carries the tale through the mountain West. Twelve editions by this printing show how well it pleased. It is a polished popular novel of love and hidden wrongs.
22152-possessed:
Cleveland Moffett, a journalist who wrote Through the Wall, published the novel Possessed in 1920. He swore the story rested largely on fact. It opens at a party in a Washington Square apartment in New York. Soft lights, low divans, and a painted ukulele set a scene of fashionable ease at Bobby Vallis's gathering.

There a sudden, dramatic prophecy is spoken over the company. The rest of the book follows that prophecy toward its strange fulfilment. Moffett mixes society comedy with the occult interests of the post-war years. Possessed belongs to the brief craze for psychic fiction that followed the Great War's losses.
22240-masterpieces-of-negro-eloquence-th:
Masterpieces of Negro Eloquence, published in 1914, gathers the best speeches delivered by Black men and women in America. Alice Moore Dunbar edited the volume, then writing as Alice Dunbar. Its speeches plead, accuse, and argue across a century of struggle. One early oration calls on Christian philanthropy to reconcile the races and points to Africa as the field for its work.

Frederick Douglass, Booker T. Washington, and many lesser-known orators stand in its pages. Church, congress, and convention platform all contribute. Dunbar meant the book as proof of a people's genius with words. It remains a handy one-volume record of African American public speech before the Harlem Renaissance.
22403-poems-of-gerard-manley-hopkins-now:
Poems of Gerard Manley Hopkins were first published long after his death. Robert Bridges, his friend, edited them with notes. Bridges kept the poems for years before letting them appear.

His verses to Hopkins call that legacy coy in his home. Hopkins's heart, he writes, once sought shelter under God's terror. Beauty and sorrow held the young poet aghast in life's wild wood. His rare talent went in disdain, ill-brokered and unpraised. Yet love of Christ, Bridges hoped, would win man's love at last. The poems that follow changed English poetry. Their springy rhythms and dense images struck readers as startlingly new.
22973-the-english-husbandman-the-first-p:
Gervase Markham offers his idle hours' work to noble readers in The English Husbandman. Its first part contains the knowledge of husbandry, the rules and maxims of farming fitted perfectly, he assures us, to the English climate. How well or ill the book is done, he writes, his lordship's wisdom must judge and correct.

Beneath the courtesy stands a practical manual of the early seventeenth century. Plowing, sowing, livestock, and seasons fill its chapters in the spelling of the day. Markham wrote for gentlemen farmers who ran real estates with real tenants. Few books show everyday Tudor and Stuart farming so closely. Readers willing to slow down for old type will find a working farm between these covers.
23198-with-no-strings-attached:
With No Strings Attached is a naval science-fiction story set aboard a United States submarine. Other boats named for Washington, Patrick Henry, and Benjamin Franklin can circle the globe without surfacing for air. For a vessel meant to run on diesel and electric power, such a feat should be rare.

A few crew members have seen what goes on in the battery room. They are, of all the crew, the most secretive and the most puzzled. That split drives the tale: most sailors serve a boat they half understand, while a small few guard a secret about how it truly runs.
a-face-illumined: Edward Payson Roe's A Face Illumined: a woman's face illumined by faith and love. Sentimental and earnest in his popular style. A favorite of 1880s readers. Roe's heroines shine with inner light, and readers loved them for it.
ancient-china-simplified: Diplomat-scholar Edward Harper Parker distills thousands of years of Chinese history into a clear, readable survey. Dynasties, philosophers, and great events pass in review, explained for Western readers with no background in the subject. Though scholarship has moved on, the book remains an engaging first map of China's immense past.
bird-neighbors-an-introductory-acquainta: Neltje Blanchan's beloved guide to 150 common birds, written for absolute beginners and rich with color plates. Her warm, plain-spoken accounts taught a generation of Americans to look up and watch. Charming and clear, it remains the friendliest first bird book ever made.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CallawayTed_Cal:
Harold Weisberg summarized the Warren Commission testimony of Ted Callaway, given March 26, 1964, and printed at volume 3, pages 351 to 357 of the hearings. Callaway was a Dallas car salesman who witnessed the aftermath of Officer J. D. Tippit's murder.

Epstein examined the raid as part of a wider pattern of police action against the Panthers. Hampton's death had already become a national controversy over how the raid was planned and carried out. Dialogue pieces let writers say in theater what they could not prove in prose. Meyer, a Washington figure later murdered, has long been tied to Kennedy in print. The piece preserves that rumor culture in dramatic form, a period artifact of the psychedelic and political undergrounds meeting.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KennedyJusticeV: Victor Navasky wrote about Robert Kennedy under a double description: as Attorney General, and as his father's son. His subject within that frame is James Landis, the former dean and presidential adviser whose fall Navasky calls a strange, sad tale. The surviving record gives the author and the titles but no date, so the piece stands as Navasky's study of Landis under Kennedy.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ReggabMohamed_R: Mohamed Reggab names this declassified US government document in the Internet Archive's holdings. The entry is bare - no year, no department, no precis. Public text unlocated. For now it is a name attached to a government file.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Ag:
Agustín Edwards owned El Mercurio, Chile's most powerful newspaper, and backed the 1973 coup against Salvador Allende. Agustin Edwards: A Declassified Obituary writes his life again from the secret record.

An ordinary obituary repeats a public reputation. A declassified one can add what the files show: Edwards's dealings with the CIA and his role in the campaign against Allende's government. The briefing book uses his death as the moment to publish that record. For readers of Chile's history, it corrects the polite version of a media magnate's life with documents.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Ch:
Peter Kornbluh edited this National Security Archive briefing book, number 642, published on October 5, 2018. It marked thirty years since Chilean voters rejected General Augusto Pinochet in the historic 1988 "NO" vote. That vote ended his dictatorship and opened the way back to democracy.

Declassified United States documents in the posting showed that Pinochet had planned a violent second coup to keep his powers if he lost. Santiago's Museum of Memory and Human Rights added those documents to its permanent exhibition on the restoration of democracy. The record ties a dictator's secret plan to the public memory of how he fell.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cold-war:
Henry Kissinger served as national security adviser and secretary of state, and few American officials left a more argued-over record. This National Security Archive posting presents a declassified dossier on that record. It uses his initials, HAK, the shorthand his own staff used.

A dossier built from declassified paper lets readers judge the controversies from documents rather than from memoirs or attacks. The posting's value is that grounding: claims about Kissinger's diplomacy, secrecy, and wars can be checked against what the files actually say. The documents, rather than the legend, are allowed to speak first.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_foia_Red:
Black bars hide the words in nearly every declassified file, and this posting, dated April 2019, studies those bars themselves. Over the years the National Security Archive collected hundreds of examples of dubious secrets. Those are places where the hidden text seemed to protect embarrassment, not security.

Redaction is where openness and secrecy meet on the page. Comparing what was blacked out with what later came out shows how often caution, habit, or self-protection drove the censor's marker. For any reader of declassified records, the file is a field guide to reading the gaps as evidence too.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_henry-ki:
In the mid-1970s South Korea quietly pursued a nuclear weapons capability, including a French reprocessing plant. This briefing book, posted in April 2019, draws on recently declassified documents from the Ford administration. Henry Kissinger's State Department pressed Seoul hard on the contract.

Washington insisted that the South Koreans break their contract with France for the plant. Reprocessing produces plutonium, the material of bombs, so the plant was the heart of the dispute. The documents show an ally being forced to back down in private. They also show how much of nonproliferation diplomacy happens as quiet pressure, not public treaty talk.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_intellig:
The President's Daily Brief is the short intelligence summary written for the president each morning. James E. David edited this briefing book, posted in December 2016, on what filled those briefs in the 1960s and 1970s. Two topics appeared more than almost any others.

Soviet missile and space programs were among the most frequent subjects briefed to the president. That frequency is itself a finding: it shows where American anxiety sat during the Cold War, in rockets and orbits. A run of daily briefs lets readers watch the arms race through the one document the president was sure to see.

For years the Soviet Union beamed microwaves at the American embassy in Moscow, and the reason stayed mysterious. Peter Kornbluh and William Burr edited this briefing book, posted in September 2022. It opens a declassified series on the Moscow Signals, including projects code-named PANDORA and BIZARRE.

The posting appeared on the fifth anniversary of the CIA pulling agents out of Cuba over the Havana Syndrome illnesses. That timing is the argument: an older case of unexplained signals and sickness may inform a newer one. The documents give the Moscow episode, long treated as Cold War folklore, a proper paper record at last.

Secrecy And Leaks: When The US Government Prosecuted The Press - the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers. Deserves a place on the shelf.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_iran_195:
Freshly declassified State Department documents, posted in August 2017, confirm how the 1953 Iran coup began. In late 1952 the British Foreign Office approached the Truman administration more than once. London proposed a coup to overthrow Iranian Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddeq.

Two previously top secret memoranda from senior State officials describe the communications and meetings that began in October 1952. British officials worked to win American support for the plot. The coup itself came in August 1953, under a new president. These papers settle the question of who first brought the idea to Washington, and when, in the plotters' own record.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_japan-nu:
For the first time, in a declassification noted here in February 2016, the United States government officially admitted a Cold War fact long reported by others. American nuclear weapons had been stored on Okinawa, the Japanese island that hosts major United States bases. Photographs bearing on the story had been available since 1990.

Official admission matters even when a fact is widely believed. Okinawa's nuclear history sits inside a larger argument about bases, Japanese anti-nuclear feeling, and secret agreements between allies. A formal declassification moves the subject from allegation to record, and gives Japanese and American readers a shared documentary starting point.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
In January 1965 Harvard professor Henry Kissinger met top Israeli officials and came away nearly certain of something Israel denied. He told American diplomats in Tel Aviv that Israel had begun a nuclear weapons project. This briefing book, posted in November 2020, publishes that meeting record for the first time.

Its title names the twin themes: duplicity and self-deception around the American inspections of Israel's Dimona reactor in 1964 and 1965. Visits meant to verify a peaceful program were managed by the hosts and half believed by the visitors. The record lets readers watch both sides perform a check that neither side fully trusted.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p: Soviet Politburo Discussed Billion-Dollar Spy: the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cyber-vault_Taint: Tainted Trove: the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete, a single capture, dated material, filed, an obscure item. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records and readers. On the library shelves.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_iran_New_document:
In 1953, Iran's elected prime minister, Mohammad Mosaddeq, was overthrown in a coup backed by Britain and the United States. An October 2019 National Security Archive news post covers a documentary that retells that story: Coup 53, directed by Taghi Amirani and edited by the famed film editor Walter Murch.

The filmmakers built the movie from recently uncovered documents and fresh interviews, and some of those documents come from the Archive's own collection. A coup once denied or blurred has become provable on paper, and the film shows the paper on screen. For readers, the posting connects two kinds of work the Archive does: prying records loose, then watching artists turn those records into a story the public will actually sit through.
hobson-imperialism-1902-1st-ed:
John A. Hobson published Imperialism: A Study in 1902, and this entry holds the first edition text. Hobson had reported from South Africa during the Boer War. He argues that empire grows from underconsumption at home. Workers paid too little cannot buy what factories make, so surplus capital seeks outlets abroad.

Investors, not the nation, gain from the colonies their money opens. That charge shaped Lenin's later book on imperialism and Keynes's thinking too. Hobson's mix of economics and moral attack made the study a classic. A later impression of the book is also held. The first edition shows his argument in its original force.
how-members-of-congress-are-bribed: Joseph Moore's How Members of Congress Are Bribed: the muckraker's exposé. Corruption in Washington, plainly told. A reformer's pamphlet. Shocking in its day, moore's Washington exposé, corruption plainly told, a reformer's shock, the muckraker's shock.
johnny-bear-and-other-stories-from-lives:
Johnny Bear, and Other Stories from Lives of the Hunted is a book of animal tales by Ernest Thompson Seton. Johnny Bear is a queer little cub who lives with his mother, Grumpy, in Yellowstone Park. Bears around the Fountain Hotel found the country a desirable home. A steward's order to dump kitchen garbage sets the first tale moving.

The contents also promise Tito, the story of a coyote that learned how. Tito's chapters run from captivity and her brood to a race for life. A third piece asks why the chickadee goes crazy once a year. Seton writes wild animals as real characters with habits, dangers, and families. His stories helped readers see hunted creatures as lives worth understanding.
khaled:
F. Marion Crawford, a well read American who lived much in Italy, wrote this tale of Arabia in 1891. He was the most cosmopolitan romancer of his day, at home in many lands. The tale stands in the line of the Arabian Nights, which he knew well.

Khaled is a genie, one of the jinn, who is made a man for a set span of life. He wins his change for the love of a mortal maid, and must learn what it is to be human. Pain, faith, and death teach him, in a tale told with grace and calm.
martie-the-unconquered:
Kathleen Thompson Norris set Martie, the Unconquered in Monroe, California. The tale opens on a warm, windy September day after school. Four girls drift from the post office toward the drug store.

Martie Monroe and her sister Sarah live in the shabby old Monroe house. Richer girls from the Frost and Parker homes barely know them. Norris builds her story from small town rank, slow days, and a girl who will not stay beaten. School, the post office, and the soda counter mark their small world. Small slights carry weight when a town ranks each girl by her home.
melmoth-reconciled:
Honore de Balzac wrote Melmoth Reconciled, here in Ellen Marriage's English. He gave the book to the General Baron de Pommereul. The gift honors a friendship held between their fathers and sons.

Balzac opens with a strange study of one kind of man: the cashier. Such a man sits boxed behind iron bars for hours each day. He must handle wealth all day and keep no relish for it. From that portrait, Balzac builds his Paris tale of a soul's bargain passed on. Nature, he jokes, now and then makes an honest cashier. That rare man is the hinge on which the tale turns.
miss-billy-married:
Eleanor H. Porter's sequel opens with opinions and a wedding: Bertram takes Billy in marriage. The chapters then test the young couple. Titles promise a big bad quarrel, the dinner Billy tried to get, and the dinner she actually got. Calderwell asks questions, and Billy receives advice from all sides.

Billy cultivates a comfortable indifference, tries her hand at managing, and faces enormous responsibility. Ghosts walk for Bertram before the storm clears. The final chapter is called By a Baby's Hand. Porter, identified on the title page as the author of Pollyanna, continues her comedy of a spirited wife.
narrative-of-an-expedition-into-central-:
Charles Sturt led an expedition into Central Australia in 1844 through 1846. He acted under orders from Her Majesty's Government. Both volumes sit in this one ebook file. A notice of South Australia in 1847 completes the work.

Sturt dedicated the book to Earl Grey with frank words. No land fit for settlement was found, he admits. Still, he hopes the toil was not fruitless, like his Murray voyage. Plates and maps are listed but not shown in this text. Sturt's party endured heat, thirst, and a land that defied them, and his record remains a classic of exploration.
nasa-tm-19640058418-a-feasible-approach-:
Dated June 16, 1961, Part I summarizes an ad hoc task group study run from NASA Headquarters. William A Fleming chaired the group, with Addison M Rothrock as deputy. Their subject was a practical plan for a first crewed landing on the Moon in 1967.

Part I is the summary, paired with a detailed Part II. Together they present a program plan, not a single spacecraft design. The group drew members from Headquarters, the Space Task Group, Marshall, and the Lovelace Foundation. Readers get the early case for how such a landing could be organized and timed.
nasa-tm-19660009067-preliminary-results-:
Gregory R Wichorek and Bland A Stein at Langley gave early results in Atlanta in April 1965 on a coated metal sheet for heat shields. The sheet is Ta-10W, an alloy of tantalum with tungsten. A coating protects such a metal from burning away in hot air. Langley programs were studying refractory metals, metals that endure great heat, for thermal protection systems.

High temperature oxidation tests form the core of the study. Results are called preliminary, so more work was expected. A heat shield that fails lets hot gas reach the structure beneath. Coated refractory sheet promised a reusable shield, unlike shields that burn away. The study tests that promise at bench scale first.
nasa-tm-19670002025-a-preliminary-invest:
George C. Kenyon and George G. Edwards, of NASA's Ames Research Center in California, wrote this wind-tunnel memorandum, dated March 1961 as printed. It asks whether a blunt thirteen-degree half-cone re-entry shape could be reshaped to fly and land horizontally. The basic shape's best lift-to-drag ratio was only 1.7, judged too low for a horizontal landing.

The tunnel work reshaped the rear of the cone and tested vertical surfaces, canopies, a folding extra lifting surface, control surfaces, and landing gear. Contouring the rear brought very large gains in lift-to-drag ratio without large trim problems. Flaps and elevons also helped, while a landing gear and an upper canopy caused no serious harm. One complete configuration reached a trimmed lift-to-drag ratio above six, though its behavior at high subsonic speeds still needed work.
nasa-tm-19670027093-the-electromagnetic-:
V. K. Balasubrahmanyan and E. Boldt, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this July 1967 paper with R. A. R. Palmeira, of the Southwest Center for Advanced Studies in Dallas, and G. Sandri. It studies the light given off as cosmic rays lose energy in interstellar hydrogen, the gas clouds between the stars.

The authors show that the observed temperature of hydrogen atoms in those clouds fits what cosmic ray collisions would produce. The same interactions could maintain a surprisingly high electron concentration in the clouds. Glow from hydrogen atoms excited by cosmic rays should approach, but stay below, the brightness measured from the galactic disk. X-radiation thrown off when cosmic rays knock electrons out of hydrogen atoms could directly reveal the spectrum of the rays causing the ionization. The paper recommends detailed study of these non-stellar X-rays to map low-energy cosmic rays across the disk.
nasa-tm-19670029045-the-local-supergalax:
Elihu Boldt, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this paper in September 1967. It connects two things: the smooth background of X-rays seen across the sky, and the local supergalaxy, our neighborhood of galaxy clusters. Boldt asks whether the nearby supergalaxy leaves a pattern in that background.

He shows that Silk's model for a universal X-ray background leads to a measurable structure. The structure arises from the local supergalaxy itself. A telescope tuned to look for it would need a wide field of view and fine resolution. The expected signal, he finds, is about as strong as the observed diffuse background.
nasa-tm-19680000635-automated-data-colle:
Ralph D. Thomas, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, built measurement gear that runs itself. His report describes a fully programmable, automated system for Hall effect and resistivity measurements. Such measurements reveal how semiconductors carry electricity.

The apparatus controls all its conditions across a wide temperature span. It logs results both as typed copy and as punched paper tape a computer can read. Thomas applied it to cadmium sulfide films and to silicon samples of both conductivity types. He also explains a simple, reliable way to make electrical contacts to samples. Accuracy and calibration get their own discussion.
nasa-tm-19680023516-comparison-of-experi:
Francis C. Chenoweth and Fred W. Steffen of Lewis Research Center compare test and forecast heat values for a round ejector in this 1968 report. The ejector served a small turbojet engine with an afterburner at sea level test stands. Wall heat levels decide if the shroud can live through the hot exhaust.

Three film-cooling rules, all based on a sealed wall, gave the forecasts. The test ejector was not sealed, so the pair worked out a fix for heat lost by glow and by free air flow. With that fix, test and forecast values matched well. One rule ran low near the coolant slot and far too high near the shroud end. One more rule set wall heat equal to coolant heat, which proved too hopeful.
nasa-tm-19700032586-precritical-analysis:
Wendell Mayo of the Lewis Research Center wrote this analysis in September 1970. It looks ahead to critical tests of a small fast-spectrum reactor design. The core is ringed by molybdenum and tailored to a set power output.

A series of critical experiments was being run by Atomics International under contract to Lewis. The test materials included lithium, nitrogen, and two kinds of uranium. Refractory metals such as hafnium, tantalum, and tungsten were also used. Mayo's paper gives the calculations made before the tests turned critical. Such pre-checks keep a first critical run safe and tell staff what to expect.
nasa-tm-19710029231-liquid-oscillation-f:
Stephen Thornton and Frank Bugg of the Marshall Space Flight Center measured how liquid sloshes inside tilted tanks. Both worked in the Aero Astrodynamics Laboratory. The tanks were cylinders whose cross sections mixed a circular arc with a straight line. Shapes ran from fully round to nearly half round. Several matched tank outlines proposed for the space shuttle.

The team tilted each tank from upright to sixty degrees. They excited the liquid both along the tilt plane and across it. Then they recorded the natural sloshing frequency for each case. Slosh matters because moving fuel can push a rocket off course. Designers use such frequencies to tune baffles and control systems. The report gives the measured values shape by shape.
one-thousand-questions-in-california-agr:
Edward James Wickson compiled this farm handbook for California growers. Wickson taught horticulture at the University of California. He also edited the Pacific Rural Press in San Francisco. The foreword says the book is no systematic treatise. It arranges real questions readers actually asked the paper.

About seven hundred people sent in the questions, he says. Answers ran weekly in the paper's columns for years. Parts treat fruit, vegetables, grain, soils, and livestock. Later parts treat dairy, poultry, pests, and plant diseases. One sample asks if four feet of soil suits lemons. Wickson answers with alkali and moisture warnings. Practical farmers still gain clear, direct help here.
overruled:
Bernard Shaw prefaced his 1912 farce Overruled with an essay, The Alleviations of Monogamy. The preface alone is a small classic of Shavian provocation. The piece, he insists, is no argument for or against polygamy. It is a clinical study of how the thing occurs. Quite ordinary people, innocent of all unusual views, are its subjects.

Theorists who praise polygamy, Shaw observes, usually lead blameless family lives. The practical libertine is the opposite. He is severe on all other libertines, and wholly conventional in his professions. Sincerely so. Like the burglar crying stop thief, he defends himself as criminals plead not guilty. Society, Shaw concludes, punishes candor and then complains of falsehood. Beneath the essay sits a comedy of two couples caught in mutual infidelity.
pamela-or-virtue-rewarded:
Samuel Richardson's Pamela, or Virtue Rewarded is told entirely in letters. The hosted edition prints more than thirty of them in sequence. Pamela writes home to her parents. Her master, Mr. B., persecutes the servant girl. Her letters record each advance and each resistance. The publishers' note introduces Richardson himself before the letters begin.

Richardson was born in 1689 and died in London in 1761. He was a printer by trade. He rose to be master of the Stationers' Company. His skill as a letter-writer made him a novelist almost by accident. The note calls him the first of the great English novelists. Pamela's letters, written in the moment's heat, invented a new kind of fiction.
persia-revisited: The sample we host shows only the front matter of Persia Revisited, the title pages and the start of the contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page names General Sir Thomas Edward Gordon, formerly military attaché and Oriental secretary to the British legation at Tehran. The book reports a visit in 1895, with remarks on the new shah, Mozuffer-ed-Din, and the situation in Persia in 1896. The contents begin with the road from London to Baku and its oil-wells.
phases-of-faith-or-passages-from-the-his:
Francis William Newman called Phases of Faith an egotistical book in form but not in purpose. His preface, dated March 1850, explains that friends had fallen away from him on religious grounds. He writes to show them he had no choice but to follow his intellectual conclusions, reached through learning, history, and criticism.

The book traces the progress of his creed alone, not a general autobiography. Its mighty truth, he argues, is that belief and faith are different things, and no fixed creed should test a man's spiritual character. Newman, brother of the cardinal, wrote the classic Victorian record of losing orthodoxy honestly.
pitman-s-commercial-spanish-grammar-2nd-:
C. A. Toledano wrote Pitman's Commercial Spanish Grammar, issued here in a second edition dated 1917, to teach Spanish for business use. The Pitman name marks it as part of a well-known line of commercial and shorthand manuals.

The grammar begins at the very start, with the Spanish alphabet and the sound of each letter's name. It then gives the five vowel sounds. They never vary, it says, except that stressed vowels run a little longer. Everyday words show the sounds: amigo for friend, cielo for heaven, and recibo for a receipt. From such basics the student moves toward the language of trade, the book's stated commercial purpose.
shakespeare-s-bones-the-proposal-to-disi:
C. M. Ingleby published this essay with Trubner in London in 1883. Ingleby was a life trustee of Shakespeare's Birthplace and a vice president of the Royal Society of Literature. He inscribed the essay to the mayor and corporation of Stratford-upon-Avon and to the vicar of Holy Trinity church there.

Ingleby weighs a plan to dig up Shakespeare's bones and judge what they might show about his portraits. Tales of visits by the living to the dead fill out the argument. The essay shows how fiercely Victorians guarded the poet's grave, and how far science claimed a right to look inside it.
she-stands-accused:
Victor Macclure wrote these accounts of famed women who faced the law, drawn, he states, from checked sources. He dedicated the book to Rafael Sabatini. Some women in these pages were hanged or jailed; others walked free, acquitted at least in law. An opening chapter weighs the title itself.

Macclure nearly chose a joking title about fair hands stained, then saw the trap: several women were cleared, and loose words could libel. Chapters bear heads like A Fair Neck for the Maiden and Arsenic a la Bretonne. True-crime readers get period cases told with care for the record.
sir-francis-drake-revived:
Philip Nichols set forth this account of Drake's raid on the Spanish treasure town of Nombre de Dios, drawn from reports by men who sailed with him. Drake himself reviewed the tale, a 1910 Collier printing notes, and his nephew issued it. An opening essay sketches Drake's rise.

Born in Devonshire about 1540, Drake sailed to the Spanish Main by 1565 and lost much to Spain in 1567. His 1572 venture repaid that loss at Spain's storehouse. Led by native guides to a great tree in Darien, Drake first of Englishmen saw the Pacific and prayed to sail it one day.
speeches-of-the-hon-jefferson-davis-of-m: Speeches of the Honorable Jefferson Davis of Mississippi gathers talks from the summer of 1858. John Murphy and Co. printed the book at Baltimore in 1859. The contents list a Fourth of July speech at sea. Talks at Portland and Belfast in Maine follow. A speech at the state fair at Augusta stands there. An address at Faneuil Hall, a New York speech, and words before the Mississippi legislature close the list. Davis says false reports of his talks drove him to gather them.
sugar-and-spice-comical-tales-comically-:
James Johnson's Sugar and Spice, subtitled Comical Tales Comically Dressed, came out at London from Dean and Son of Fleet Street, a firm known for Christmas cards and children's books. The tales are told in comic verse, with pictures, for young readers.

The first piece opens at a party given by children with not one grown person there. The young hosts cast lots for a servant, and the lot falls on T. Good, who will not come when rung for, will not hear when called, and must be coaxed in with marmalade to carry a letter out. His grumbling speech on how rich people treat servants gives the joke a small, sharp edge.
superseded:
May Sinclair, author of The Divine Fire, published Superseded in 1906. A publishers' note explains the reissue. Sinclair wished the book republished in America. She counted it the best of her work before The Divine Fire. It had first appeared with another work. That volume was called Two Sides of a Question.

The chapters open with a prologue, Miss Quincey Stops the Way, and close with an epilogue, The Man and the Woman. Between them stand household gods, inaugural addresses, healers and regenerators, and Dr. Bastian Cautley, whose bill arrives near the end. The first scene files the girls of St. Sidwell's school out along a corridor under their teachers' eyes, with Miss Quincey barring the way.
superstition-unveiled:
Charles Southwell, author of Supernaturalism Exploded, published Superstition Unveiled at London through Edward Truelove in 1854, abridging the work himself from his Apology for Atheism. A motto at the front bids readers know their gods before they worship them.

Southwell argues that religion bears on every part of life, and that the tie between faith and politics is far closer than most people think. Religious error, he claims, is the unseen base of political injustice, and a people fettered by superstition cannot win political freedom. He mocks reformers who see Islam's grip on Constantinople yet act as if Christianity had nothing to do with the politics of England. The tract is blunt, eager freethought writing.
sustained-honor-the-age-of-liberty-estab:
John R. Musick's Sustained Honor, subtitled The Age of Liberty Established, forms Volume X of The Real America in Romance, printed in 1909 with illustrations by Freeland A. Carter. The series retells the nation's founding as historical novels, and this volume covers the age when American liberty was made secure.

Musick's preface argues that written history is too scholastic for most readers: dignified and formal, it skips the details of individual life and so gives a stiff, unnatural picture of the past. Well-written fiction, he claims, is drawn from nature and experience, arranging the facts of life like chessmen in new but natural positions. The novel that follows dresses the Revolution's settlement in scenes, plots, and private lives.
sword-blades-and-poppy-seed:
Amy Lowell's Sword Blades and Poppy Seed is a book of poems. Lowell was a Massachusetts poet. A French epigraph from Henri de Regnier opens it. The lines treat medals engraved in silver, gold, and bronze. Some are made of fragile clay. Lowell's own preface argues against the notion that poets are simply born.

No one expects a man to make a chair without first learning how, she writes, yet people suppose verses burst from a poet's overflowing heart of themselves. In fact the poet must learn his trade with the same painstaking care as the cabinet-maker, and master the written word before his thoughts can reach a reader. The poems that follow, in verse and prose-poem forms, put that craft doctrine to work in bright, hard images.
tarzan-the-untamed:
Edgar Rice Burroughs wrote Tarzan the Untamed as a war-time Tarzan novel in twenty-four chapters, set on the East African front. Chapter heads run from Murder and Pillage and In the German Lines to The Walled City and The Flight from Xuja.

Chapter one tracks Hauptmann Fritz Schneider, a German officer, as he sweats through dark forest with worn porters. His men drive the porters on with bayonet points and rifle butts, a sight that fixes the foe's cruelty at the start. Tarzan then wages his own grim war of revenge and mercy. Readers get lions, lost fliers, and a hidden city mixed with spy hunts and trench-age foes.
the-beautiful-and-damned: F. Scott Fitzgerald is named as author, with a date of 1922, on a title page followed by a publisher's list of his books. The list groups novels, stories, and essays, naming The Great Gatsby, Tender Is the Night, and This Side of Paradise among the novels. An unfinished novel, The Last Tycoon, is listed with a foreword by Edmund Wilson. No chapter, preface, or opening text of the novel itself appears in these pages.
the-betrothed:
An introduction dated 1832 frames a tale issued as part of Tales of the Crusaders. Its author admits the series title was chosen more by friends' advice than by his own taste. The name Crusaders, he feared, would raise grand images no tale could fill.

He also muses on titles, saying a taking title helps a bookseller sell an edition, while authors should seek lasting fame. The first tale, he explains, is less an incident of the Crusades than a story shaped by the cast of mind those ventures spread. Confusion among families was, he notes, one evil that followed their great weight in the age.
the-botanical-magazine-vol-01-or-flower-: William Curtis wrote The Botanical Magazine; or, Flower-Garden Displayed, Volume I. Curtis had also made the Flora Londinensis. The title page, states the plan of the work. The most fine foreign plants grown in open ground, in the green-house, and in the stove are shown in their true colors. Each plant gets its name, class, and kind marks by the system of Linnaeus, its home ground, and its time of bloom. The best ways to raise it are added, for ladies, gentlemen, and gardeners.
the-botanical-magazine-vol-02-or-flower-: Volume II of The Botanical Magazine; or, Flower-Garden Displayed, by William Curtis, holds the same title page as the first book of the set. Curtis is named as the maker of the Flora Londinensis. The page states that the most fine foreign plants are shown in their true colors. Names, class, order, and kind marks follow the system of Linnaeus. Places of growth and times of bloom are set down, with the best ways to raise the plants.
the-botanical-magazine-vol-03-or-flower-: The Botanical Magazine; or, Flower-Garden Displayed, Volume III, by William Curtis, opens with a title page much like those of the first two books. A verse from Cowper stands on it,. The page pledges true-color plates of the most fine foreign plants. It pledges names, class, order, and kind marks by the system of Linnaeus. It adds each plant's home ground, its time of bloom, and the best ways to raise it. The work speaks to ladies, gentlemen, and gardeners.
the-botanical-magazine-vol-04-or-flower-: William Curtis made The Botanical Magazine; or, Flower-Garden Displayed, and Volume IV bears his name as maker of the Flora Londinensis. Its title page is much the same as in the first books of the set. A verse from Thomson stands at the front. The page says the most fine foreign plants are drawn in their true colors. Names and kind marks follow Linnaeus, with home grounds and bloom times. Best means of culture are added.
the-botanical-magazine-vol-05-or-flower-: Volume V of The Botanical Magazine; or, Flower-Garden Displayed, by William Curtis, again opens with the set's shared title page. A head note says old spellings of place names were left as first printed. The page promises plates in true colors of the most fine foreign plants grown in open ground, the green-house, and the stove. It promises names, class, order, and kind marks after Linnaeus. Home grounds, bloom times, and best ways of culture are to be added.
the-churches-of-coventry-a-short-history: Frederic W. Woodhouse wrote this short history of Coventry and its medieval remains, published in London by George Bell and Sons in 1909 with forty illustrations. Only the title page and the start of the contents are present here. The contents open with the monastery and city, then the ruins of the priory and cathedral church, then St. Michael's Church and Holy Trinity Church, each treated by history, exterior, and interior.Its inside pages are not among what is present.
the-closet-of-sir-kenelm-digby-knight-op:
Sir Kenelm Digby's closet of recipes, newly edited by Anne Macdonell, was published in London by Philip Lee Warner in 1910. The frontispiece shows Digby after a portrait by Sir Anthony Vandyke at Windsor Castle. Old spellings, the transcribers note, are left as they stand, inconsistencies included.

The contents map a household treasury in print. Receipts for mead, metheglin, and other drinks run first, followed by cookery receipts, then a section called The Table. An appendix adds more receipts, an account of the powder of sympathy, and a list of the herbs and flowers named in the text. Notes, a glossary, and an index of receipts close the volume. Macdonell's introduction and notes frame Digby's kitchen and stillroom knowledge for modern readers, keeping a seventeenth-century gentleman's practice open to study.
the-commercial-products-of-the-vegetable: P. L. Simmonds wrote this practical treatise and handbook on plant products, dated 1854 in Roman numerals, for colonists, manufacturers, merchants, and consumers. Its long title promises the cultivation, preparation for shipment, and commercial value of substances from trees and plants in tropical and sub-tropical regions. Only the title page and the start of a subscribers' list are present here, naming the African Steam Ship Company and the Assam Company among the buyers. No chapter text follows.
the-complete-english-tradesman-1839-ed:
Daniel Defoe wrote this guide for tradesmen, first published at London in 1726 and shown here in an Edinburgh edition of 1839. The contents open with the tradesman in his preparations while an apprentice, then his letter writing and his trading style. Later chapters treat his acquaintance with business in general, diligence, and the danger of over-trading.

The second half of the list is a anatomy of ruin. Defoe treats the tradesman in distress and becoming bankrupt, then the ordinary occasions of tradesmen's ruin. Innocent diversions, extravagant and expensive living, and marrying too soon each get a chapter as steps toward disaster. Leaving business to servants closes what is present. The order is the argument: success starts in training and daily habits, while failure creeps in through pleasure, show, and neglect. Apprentices and young shopkeepers were the book's first audience.
the-coquette-or-the-history-of-eliza-wha:
The Coquette, or the History of Eliza Wharton, bills itself as a novel founded on fact, written by a lady of Massachusetts. This edition carries a historical preface with a memoir of the author. The preface writer says the romance came out not long after the events it records, and that its author was well schooled for the times and the wife of a much-liked clergyman.

By that account, the book ran through a score of editions and was found in nearly every New England cottage beside the family Bible. It took first place in interest among American novels, the preface claims, at a time when the day's reading was anything but light. The writer asks readers to approach the real people behind the tale with a tender heart and a gentle hand.
the-damned:
Algernon Blackwood's The Damned, dated 1914, opens in talk between Bill, the narrator, and his sister Frances. Bill is over forty and set in his ways, with heavy work on hand. He doubts he could work at the house they are asked to visit, among a crowd of unassorted people.

Frances answers that Mabel Franklyn's invitation names no other guests; she gathers Mabel is alone, and lonely besides. Bill pictures the banker's widow from her neat, childish handwriting: timid, slight, with pale grey eyes and the air of a backward child. He recalls her late husband's roomy country mansion, altered to his needs. Its bare spread suggests a wing of Kensington Museum fitted up for eating and sleeping, unlike the poky Chelsea flat he and Frances keep.
the-days-of-mohammed:
Anna May Wilson's The Days of Mohammed was published by the David C. Cook Publishing Company under an 1897 copyright. In her preface Wilson states one aim. It is to bring out the fact that the heaven-life can begin on earth. Helpful thoughts on reaching that life are shown in the careers of her characters.

She says she worked from the best books on Mohammed and Arabia to keep the historical basis strictly correct. Her debts run to Irving, Burton, and the Rev. Geo. Bush, to the travels of Burckhardt, Joseph Pitts, Ludovico Bartema, and Giovanni Finati, Each made the pilgrimage to Medina and Mecca. Her debts run also to Prof. Max Muller's synopsis in the front of Palmer's translation of the Koran. She casts the little book forth like a pebble whose ripples may reach a weary heart.
the-development-of-the-european-nations-: J. Holland Rose, fellow of Christ's College, Cambridge and author of lives of Napoleon and William Pitt, published The Development of the European Nations, 1870-1914, in a fifth edition dated 1915. A Virgil motto heads the title page, and Rose dedicates the work to his wife, without whose help it could not have been completed. The contents open with the causes of the Franco-German War and a chapter from Worth to Gravelotte. Only the front matter and part of the contents are present here.
the-dragon-and-the-raven-or-the-days-of-:
G. A. Henty's The Dragon and the Raven; or, The Days of King Alfred opens with a preface to his boy readers. In days of peace, he says, it is hard to picture England overrun for years by pagan Danes who slew and plundered at will. He asks lads to think of a mutiny in India gone wrong, with whites at the mercy of the foe.

His hero Edmund fights beside Alfred from flight to triumph. Chapters name Croyland's massacre, the ship Dragon, Athelney, and Paris. Henty blends school history with a fast tale of courage.
the-earth-trembled: E. P. Roe's novel The Earth Trembled stands as volume fifteen of his works in this printing. Its contents open with Mary Wallingford, Love's Agony, and Uncle Sheba's Experience. Then come Mara, her purpose, and a vow of never forget, never forgive. Later chapters bring Miss Ainsley, Captain Bodine, and two little bakers. No story text appears in these pages. Only the contents list is present.
the-education-of-the-negro-prior-to-1861: C. G. Woodson's The Education of the Negro Prior to 1861, dated 1919, is present here as a title page and contents list. The chapters run from Religion with Letters to Learning in Spite of Opposition. Later heads cover city schools, higher learning, and trade training. An appendix of documents, a source list, and an index are also named. No chapter text appears in these pages.
the-emancipated:
George Gissing's The Emancipated spreads its cast across Italy and England in two full parts. First heads name northerners in sunlight, Cecily Doran, a boarding house on the Mergellina at Naples, and Miriam's brother. Later come the artist astray, captive travellers, the martyr, and a dead city.

Part two turns to a corner of society, the proprieties defended, and the denyers in England. Young folk freed from strict faith test what freedom costs. Gissing writes of belief, art, and marriage with a cool, keen eye. Naples sun gilds the start; England tests the end.
the-forme-of-cury-a-roll-of-ancient-engl:
The Forme of Cury is a roll of old English cookery put together about 1390 by the master cooks of King Richard II. It was later shown to Queen Elizabeth by Edward, Lord Stafford.

S. Pegge edited the roll and wrote the letter that opens this printing, dated St. George's Day, 1780, to Gustavus Brander, who held the work. Notes and a full glossary help readers through old words and lost dishes. The book keeps the fare of a king's hall: sauces, roasts, and spiced dishes of a rich court, set down by the men who cooked them.
the-half-hearted: The Half-Hearted, John Buchan's novel. The half-hearted hero. This book preserves that tale. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
the-light-that-failed: Rudyard Kipling wrote his novel of an artist going blind, and its front pages carry a famous dedication in verse to his mother. Only the contents, that dedication poem, and a one line preface are present here, stating that the story follows the form in which the writer first conceived it. The poem vows that a mother love, tears, and prayers would follow a son through hanging, drowning, or damnation. The novel itself stays beyond the pages held in this record beyond those front pages.
the-story-of-siegfried: James Baldwin retells the Norse legend of Siegfried — the dragon-slayer, the hero of the Nibelungen — for young readers. Gods, giants, and a cursed ring fill this stirring introduction to the North's greatest hero-tale. The myths that inspired Wagner, made thrillingly accessible.
wrecked-but-not-ruined: Wrecked but not Ruined, R, m, ballantyne's castaway tale, the wreck's survivors. This book preserves that adventure. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
